headline: India's Tiger Comeback Requires New Wildlife Corridors
meta_description: As Bengal tiger numbers more than double since 1972, India builds wildlife underpasses and overpasses to protect dispersing populations through human-dominated…
summary_short: India's tiger population has more than doubled to 3,682, but now the country must protect critical forest corridors as the big cats disperse from reserves into fragmente…
body:
India's conservation efforts have achieved a remarkable milestone: Bengal tiger numbers have more than doubled since 1972, from roughly 1,827 to an estimated 3,682 as of 2022. But success brings a new challenge. As tigers rebound and protected habitats reach capacity, the cats must disperse into human-dominated landscapes—and India is racing to protect their pathways before expanding road infrastructure seals them off. The solution lies in forest corridors, especially structures like the Teen Pani underpass beneath National Highway 72 in Rajaji Tiger Reserve, where wildlife from mice to elephants pass safely under rushing traffic.

India has built more wildlife mitigation structures—overpasses and underpasses—than any other Asian country. Since 2017, the nation has constructed the world's 10 largest wildlife underpasses and overpasses, reflecting an unprecedented investment in wildlife protection by a developing economy. The Terai Arc landscape, a 51,000-square-kilometer string of protected areas along the Himalayan foothills, now supports around 560 tigers—more than triple the population from two decades ago. But experts say that of the 19 corridors tigers use in this landscape, at least 10 need urgent attention.

The urgency is real. Even as India reconnects habitats through these ingenious underpasses and overpasses, the country continues rapidly expanding road infrastructure and clearing forested land. A male tiger's home range can span up to 200 square kilometers, making habitat fragmentation particularly threatening. Without protected corridors allowing tigers to roam, hunt, find water, and breed with distant populations, the genetic diversity that safeguards them against extinction erodes. In a country of 1.4 billion people, where the economy has grown 6-7% annually over the past decade, preserving these slender jungle pathways represents a choice to let wild tigers thrive alongside human progress.
quick_facts: Bengal tiger numbers more than doubled from 1,827 in 1972 to 3,682 in 2022
India built world's 10 largest wildlife underpasses and overpasses since 2017
Teen Pani underpass under National Highway 72 allows safe passage for all species
Terai Arc landscape supports 560 tigers, triple the population from 20 years ago
Male tigers require home ranges up to 200 square kilometers to thrive
